spoken.said: This is a spoken cheat sheet on living with home after a deploy: part two of three on home's deploy. Home is the server on your own network. Reach for it when you want to restart something on home, run a compose command, change a compose file, or restore the database by hand. By the end, you'll know which commands run the release last applied, what the guard refuses and why, how to restore a backup safely, and what isn't in the release yet. It is as of November fifteenth, twenty twenty-six, checked against the server repository, which holds home's services, and the some-ui repository, which holds the web app. Later commits may have moved things, and every card is stamped with the commits it was checked against.

spoken.chapter: Chapter one. After make home-deploy, there is nothing left to start.
spoken.narration: make home-deploy brings the release up and waits for every service, so there's no make up to run afterwards. Once every service runs the release and is ready, it writes applied dot json. From then on, make up and make compose run that release, from its own tree, never the release dot json in your checkout. That's why a git pull changes nothing they start: a pulled main reaches home only when make home-deploy applies it. The mistake to expect is pulling, running make up, and wondering why nothing moved.

params.title: make up and make compose run the release last applied

rows.note: Under the deploy's lock, so never during a deploy.
One that may change containers holds the lock; ps, logs and exec don't.
Starts nothing, reads the checkout. Then commit, push, make home-deploy.

spoken.chapter: Chapter two. The commands you'll use on home.
spoken.narration: To restart what runs, use make up. It runs under the deploy's lock, so never during a deploy. For any other compose command, use make compose, with ARGS set to the command in quotes. A command that may change containers holds the lock too; ps, logs and exec don't. If no release has been applied yet, both refuse, and name make home-deploy. When you change a file under deploy slash home, run make preflight first. It starts nothing, and reads your checkout. Then commit, push, and run make home-deploy.

params.kicker: TERMINAL · THE GUARD, AT RUN TIME
params.title: What make compose refuses on home

lines.comment: # each moves one image apart from its release
# a shell's COMPOSE_FILE is dropped; each refusal has a test

spoken.chapter: Chapter three. The guard at run time: what make compose refuses.
spoken.narration: On home, make compose runs envctl compose with the home role, and it refuses anything that would move one image apart from its release. That means pull, build and watch; dash dash build on any command but exec; up with dash dash watch or dash w; an up that names services; and dash f or dash dash project-directory, which point at another stack. A COMPOSE underscore FILE set in your shell is dropped. Each refusal has a test. When one of these is refused, the guard is working: the way to change what runs is a new release.

params.kicker: CHEAT SHEET · THE GUARD, IN REVIEW
params.title: Lint's Home guard refuses, on every PR

rows.note: Every home service's image is this, filled from the release.
Local builds live in dev.build.yml, which home never loads.
Judged by envctl's rule, ported word for word.

spoken.chapter: Chapter four. The guard in review: what lint refuses on every pull request.
spoken.narration: The same rule is checked before anything merges. Lint's home guard refuses a foreign image: every home service's image is the IMAGE variable for that service, filled from the release. It refuses a local build key, since local builds live in dev dot build dot yml, which home never loads. It refuses a floating tag, latest, anywhere, and an entry without an at sha256 digest. It also reads the commands written in docs, such as pull, build and watch, and judges them by envctl's rule, ported word for word. So a doc can't teach a command home would refuse.

spoken.chapter: Chapter five. Why there is only one way onto home.
spoken.narration: On November eleventh, twenty twenty-six, you said it plainly: there's only one way to deploy this, and we need all of them to be up. An image pulled, built or floated alone makes a set nobody checked. A release is checked as a set, each requires label met by a provides label. Continuous integration checks it from the registry, and the deploy checks it again from the pulled images. The case that taught this: a release of www, the web app, went out without its matching renderer, and every preview broke. The reasoning is written in docs slash release dot md.

params.title: Never automatic: a backup lacks the writes made after it

lines.comment: # never delete it, and never a -before- name: the prune would count it
# the release last applied, not the checkout's
# a run that ends with exit 3 names the backup that start took

spoken.chapter: Chapter six. Restoring the database by hand, only when you choose.
spoken.narration: A restore is never automatic, because a backup lacks every write made after it. When you do choose one, the order matters. First, stop file host: make compose, with ARGS stop file-host. Second, move the current database, hopium dot db, into the backups folder under a name of its own. Never delete it, and never give it a name with dash before dash in it, or the backup pruning would count it. Third, copy the backup you want to hopium dot db. Last, run make up, which starts the release last applied, not the checkout's. A deploy that ended with exit three names the backup that start took.

spoken.chapter: Chapter seven. What isn't in the release yet.
spoken.narration: Two things don't move with make home-deploy yet. The web app, www, is started from the some-ui checkout with its own compose file today, so a deploy doesn't move it. It joins the release with a server change that is planned and not landed, along with its requires labels. The résumé renderer, resume-render, joins with the same change; it isn't in release dot json today. Both are marked with an empty square: planned, not built.

spoken.chapter: Chapter eight. Reading the badges on these cards.
spoken.narration: Each claim on a card carries a badge saying how far to trust it. A filled square is on main, the default branch, at the commit the card is stamped with. A half-filled square is an open pull request. An empty square is planned, not built. A triangle is a known gap. A raised hand is a step only you do. Trust the filled squares, and check the others against the repository before you rely on them.

spoken.chapter: Chapter nine. How stale is this?
spoken.narration: All of this was true on the day it was stamped. If what you see differs, the sources are the server README's section on deploying to home, and docs slash release dot md, and when they disagree, the release doc wins, because it is the one meant to be kept current. Compare the stamped commit with main to see how far things have moved.

spoken.said: That's life after the deploy. Next time, use make up to restart, make compose for anything else, and make preflight before you commit a change to deploy slash home. If a command is refused, that's the guard, and docs slash release dot md says why. Part one of this series covers the deploy itself.
